{{Short description|Set of numbers used in the smoothsort algorithm}}
{{primary sources|date=July 2017}}
The '''Leonardo numbers''' are a sequence of numbers given by the recurrence:
:<math> 
  L(n) = 
  \begin{cases}
    1                       & \mbox{if } n = 0 \\
    1                       & \mbox{if } n = 1 \\
    L(n - 1) + L(n - 2) + 1 & \mbox{if } n > 1 \\
  \end{cases}
 </math>

[[Edsger W. Dijkstra]]<ref>{{Cite web|title=E.W.Dijkstra Archive: Fibonacci numbers and Leonardo numbers. (EWD 797)|url=https://www.cs.utexas.edu/users/EWD/transcriptions/EWD07xx/EWD797.html|access-date=2020-08-11|website=www.cs.utexas.edu}}</ref> used them as an integral part of his [[smoothsort]] [[algorithm]],<ref>{{Cite EWD|796a|Smoothsort – an alternative to sorting in situ}}</ref>  and also analyzed them in some detail.<ref>{{Cite web|title=E.W.Dijkstra Archive: Smoothsort, an alternative for sorting in situ (EWD 796a)|url=https://www.cs.utexas.edu/users/EWD/transcriptions/EWD07xx/EWD796a.html|access-date=2020-08-11|website=www.cs.utexas.edu}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Leonardo Number - GeeksforGeeks |url=https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/leonardo-number/ |access-date=2022-10-08 |website=www.geeksforgeeks.org|date=18 October 2017}}</ref>

A '''Leonardo prime''' is a '''Leonardo number''' that is also [[Prime number|prime]].

==Name==

The term "Leonardo number" was coined by Dijkstra<ref>{{Cite web|title=E.W.Dijkstra Archive: Fibonacci numbers and Leonardo numbers. (EWD 797)|url=https://www.cs.utexas.edu/users/EWD/transcriptions/EWD07xx/EWD797.html|access-date=2020-08-11|website=www.cs.utexas.edu}}</ref>{{r|g=nb|r=The [[OEIS]] lists Dijkstra's paper as the first reference to the sequence. {{OEIS|id=A145912}}}}, and the derivation is not given explicitly.  Given the close relationship to the famous sequence credited to [[Leonardo Fibonacci]], he may have considered the subject trivial.  There is no known nor likely connection to [[Leonardo da Vinci]], the most common subject of that [[mononym]].

==Values==
The first few Leonardo numbers are
:1, 1, 3, 5, 9, 15, 25, 41, 67, 109, 177, 287, 465, 753, 1219, 1973, 3193, 5167, 8361, ... {{OEIS|id=A001595}}

The first few Leonardo primes are
:[[3]], [[5]], [[41 (number)|41]], [[67 (number)|67]], [[109 (number)|109]], 1973, 5167, 2692537, 11405773, 126491971, 331160281, 535828591, 279167724889, 145446920496281, 28944668049352441, 5760134388741632239, 63880869269980199809, 167242286979696845953, 597222253637954133837103, ... {{OEIS|id=A145912}}

==Modulo cycles==
The Leonardo numbers form a cycle in any modulo <math>n  \geq 2</math>. An easy way to see it is:
* If a pair of numbers modulo <math>n</math> appears twice in the sequence, then there is a cycle.
* If we assume the main statement is false, using the previous statement, then it would imply there are an infinite number of distinct pairs of numbers between <math>0</math> and <math>n-1</math>, which is false since there are <math>n^2</math> such pairs.
The cycles for <math>n \leq 8</math> are:

|}
The cycle always end on the pair <math>(1,n-1)</math>, as it is the only pair which can precede the pair <math>(1,1)</math>.

==Expressions==
*The following equation applies:
:<math>L(n)=2L(n-1)-L(n-3)</math>
{{Math proof|title=Proof|proof=<math>L(n)=L(n-1)+L(n-2)+1=L(n-1)+L(n-2)+1+L(n-3)-L(n-3)=2L(n-1)-L(n-3)</math>}}

==Relation to Fibonacci numbers==
The Leonardo numbers are related to the [[Fibonacci number]]s by the relation <math>L(n) = 2 F(n+1) - 1, n \ge 0</math>.

From this relation it is straightforward to derive a [[closed-form expression]] for the Leonardo numbers, analogous to Binet's formula for the Fibonacci numbers:
:<math>L(n) = 2 \frac{\varphi^{n+1} - \psi^{n+1}}{\varphi - \psi}- 1 = \frac{2}{\sqrt 5} \left(\varphi^{n+1} - \psi^{n+1}\right) - 1 = 2F(n+1) - 1</math>

where the [[golden ratio]] <math>\varphi = \left(1 + \sqrt 5\right)/2</math> and <math>\psi = \left(1 - \sqrt 5\right)/2</math> are the roots of the [[quadratic polynomial]] <math>x^2 - x - 1 = 0</math>.

==Leonardo polynomials ==
The Leonardo polynomials <math> L_{n}(x) </math> is defined by <ref>Kalika Prasad, Munesh Kumari (2024): The Leonardo polynomials and their algebraic properties. ''Proc. Indian Natl. Sci. Acad.'' https://doi.org/10.1007/s43538-024-00348-0</ref>
:<math>L_{n+2}(x)=xL_{n+1}(x)+L_{n}(x)+x </math> with <math>L_{0}(x) = 1, L_{1}(x)=2x-1. </math>

Equivalently, in homogeneous form, the Leonardo polynomials can be written as
:<math>L_{n+3}(x)= (x+1)L_{n+2}(x)-(x-1)L_{n+1}(x)-L_{n}(x):</math>
where <math>L_{0}(x)=1, L_{1}(x)=2x-1 </math> and <math> L_{2}(x)=2x^2+1.</math>

==Examples of Leonardo polynomials  ==
:<math>L_{0}(x)=1 \,</math>
:<math>L_{1}(x)=2x-1\,</math>
:<math>L_{2}(x)=2x^2+1\,</math>
:<math>L_{3}(x)=2x^3+4x-1\,</math>
:<math>L_{4}(x)=2x^4 + 6x^2 + 1 \,</math>
:<math>L_{5}(x)=2x^5+8x^3+6x-1 \,</math>
:<math>L_{6}(x)=2x^6+10x^4+12x^2+1\,</math>
:<math>L_{7}(x)=2x^7+12x^5+20x^3+8x-1 \,</math>
:<math>L_{8}(x)=2 x^8+14 x^6+30 x^4+20 x^2+1 \,</math>
:<math>L_{9}(x)=2 x^9+16 x^7+42 x^5 + 40x^3 + 10x-1 \,</math>
:<math>L_{10}(x)=2 x^{10}+18 x^8+56 x^6+70 x^4+30 x^2+1\,</math> 
:<math>L_{11}(x)=2 x^{11}+20 x^9+72 x^7+112 x^5+70 x^3+12x-1 \,</math>

Substituting <math>x=1</math> in the above polynomials gives the Leonardo numbers and setting <math>x=k</math> gives the <math>k</math>-Leonardo numbers.<ref>Kalika Prasad, Munesh Kumari (2025): The generalized k-Leonardo numbers: a non-homogeneous generalization of the Fibonacci numbers, ''Palestine Journal of Mathematics, 14.''</ref>
